model.name: Evidence / Rationale
model.purpose: Provide a format-neutral, attachable structure that records traceable support for a claim or decision: what supports it, by what reasoning, on whose authority, with what integrity, how strong the support is, and how it can be re-checked, contested, retained or withdrawn.
model.scope_statement: This mixin is attached to a host record that already asserts something (a claim, decision, classification, requirement or measurement held in a sibling model). It supplies the support apparatus around that assertion: typed support relations to evidence items, the inference/warrant and assumptions that license the conclusion, counter-evidence and its resolution, evidence identity, anchoring into sources, acquisition and custody, provenance and time, cryptographic integrity and verification, quality appraisal and sufficiency, and the governance surface (authority, rights, access, retention, lifecycle, interoperability). It never carries the propositional content of the claim itself and never duplicates the bibliographic record of a source, the agent registry or the audit-log infrastructure.
in_scope: Typed support and counter-support relations between evidence items and a supported claim or decision
Reasoning apparatus: warrant/inference, argumentation scheme, assumptions, scope conditions, alternatives considered and rejected
Evidence item identity, form/modality, anchoring into a source location and state, and excerpt fidelity
Acquisition method, instrument, and chain of custody including auditability, repeatability and reproducibility
Provenance, attribution, independence/conflict of interest, and separated event/observation/record/assertion times
Cryptographic content binding, signatures/attestations, trusted timestamps and verification events
Certainty grading against a declared scheme, bias and limitations, sufficiency thresholds and corroboration
Governance of the support record: ownership, approving authority, rights, access classification, redaction, retention, legal hold, lifecycle states and retraction
Declared alignments and exchange packaging to external provenance, assurance-case, credential and attestation models
out_of_scope: The propositional content, truth value or semantics of the supported claim itself (belongs to the parent knowledge/claim model)
The full bibliographic or catalogue record of a source document, dataset or publication (sibling source/citation model)
The agent, organisation and role registry that identifiers here resolve into (sibling agent/party model)
General-purpose provenance/lineage of arbitrary artefacts not offered in support of a claim (sibling provenance model)
Audit-log and telemetry infrastructure design, log shipping and SIEM operation
Legal case management, court procedure, disclosure workflow and forensic investigation case files
Evidence synthesis statistics: meta-analysis, pooling, effect-size estimation and study design
Dialogue and argumentation protocols (turn taking, burden shifting in dialogue games)
Trust or reputation scoring of agents and sources as a standalone scored model
Cryptographic key management, PKI operation and trust-list curation

boundary_notes.distinction: The parent holds the assertion; this mixin holds why the assertion is held. An assurance case separates the top-level claim from the structured argumentation and the evidence and assumptions underlying it, so the claim must remain addressable independently of its support.

This model references a source by identifier and adds a locator, selector and captured state; it does not carry title, authorship, edition or catalogue metadata. Web Annotation separates the Target resource from the Specific Resource plus Selector used to address part of it.

PROV describes generation, derivation and attribution for any entity. This mixin uses that vocabulary only for entities offered in support of a claim, and additionally records the assertion of support itself, which PROV does not model.

A verifiable credential is itself a signed claim container whose optional evidence property describes how the issuer verified claims before issuance. A credential may be an evidence item here, but credential issuance, holding and presentation are governed elsewhere.

Automatically generated logs are a source of evidence items and are separately mandated with their own retention floors; the logging subsystem, its content requirements and its retention schedule belong to the log model, not to this mixin.

ISO/IEC 27037 governs identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of potential digital evidence by designated roles. This mixin records the custody and integrity facts needed to reason about admissibility, not the forensic process, tooling competence regime or investigation case file.

The decision, its options and its outcome live in the decision model. This mixin supplies the rationale, alternatives-rejected reasons and supporting evidence attached to that decision, in the same way an architecture description carries rationale separately from the architecture it describes.

An observation's method, unit, uncertainty and sensor semantics belong to the measurement model. Here an observation is treated as an evidence item with an acquisition record and an appraisal, not re-specified.

sources.title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
sources.relevance: Normative OWL2 vocabulary for Entity, Activity, Agent and the properties wasDerivedFrom, wasGeneratedBy, wasAttributedTo, used, hadPrimarySource, wasQuotedFrom, wasRevisionOf and prov:Bundle; grounds derivation, primary-source and quotation semantics for evidence items.

sources.title: PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model
sources.relevance: Defines attribution, association, delegation, invalidation, specialization/alternate, generation/usage/start/end times, and Bundle as an entity enabling provenance-of-provenance so that the support record itself can be attributed and dated.

sources.title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
sources.relevance: Defines the optional evidence property (how an issuer verified claims before issuance), proof/securing mechanisms, issuer, validFrom/validUntil and credentialStatus, and states that verification of a credential does not imply evaluation of the truth of its claims — a key separation between integrity and validity.

sources.title: Web Annotation Data Model
sources.relevance: Body/Target model, motivation vocabulary, Specific Resource with FragmentSelector, TextQuoteSelector, TextPositionSelector, RangeSelector, CssSelector, XPathSelector, plus TimeState and creator/created/generator; grounds precise anchoring of an excerpt into a source and pinning of the source state.

sources.title: Structured Assurance Case Metamodel (SACM), Version 2.3
sources.relevance: Defines an assurance case as a set of auditable claims, arguments and evidence created to support a claim that a system or service satisfies particular requirements; grounds the separation of claim, argumentation and evidence artefacts and the auditability requirement.

sources.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2:2022 Systems and software engineering — Systems and software assurance — Part 2: Assurance case
sources.relevance: Specifies minimum structure and content of an assurance case: a top-level claim, systematic argumentation, and the evidence and explicit assumptions underlying it; defines inference as a reasoning step deriving a claim from subclaims under a specified context, with confidence depending on the validity of the inference expressed as a justification and on confidence in the premises. Explicitly does not mandate a concrete or graphical representation.

sources.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 Software, systems and enterprise — Architecture description
sources.relevance: Specifies required content for architecture descriptions and distinguishes the entity of interest from the description expressing it; supplies the precedent that rationale, concerns and correspondences are recorded as first-class description content separate from the thing described.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 27037:2012 Information technology — Security techniques — Guidelines for identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
sources.relevance: Defines the four handling processes (identification, collection, acquisition, preservation) and the principles of auditability, repeatability and reproducibility, and requires an unbroken chain of custody maintained across the lifetime of the evidence and beyond, covering physical, logical (hashes, seals, qualified timestamps) and documentary custody.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
sources.relevance: Mandatory timestamp profile: four-digit year, seconds, and a mandatory numeric offset or Z; distinguishes -00:00 (UTC known, local offset unknown) from Z/+00:00. Governs every time value in this model.

sources.title: RFC 3161: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)
sources.relevance: A TSA acting as trusted third party establishes evidence that a datum existed before a particular time; defines messageImprint, genTime, accuracy, nonce and serialNumber and requires a trustworthy time source and audit trails allowing genuine tokens to be distinguished from backdated ones.

sources.title: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification, Version 2.2
sources.organization: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
sources.relevance: Manifest = assertions + a signed claim + claim signature; requires at least one hard binding so a validator can confirm the manifest belongs with the asset and the asset is unmodified; defines hashed URIs (location plus hash), created vs gathered assertions, ingredient manifests for derived works, and trusted time-stamps enabling indefinite validation after credential expiry.

sources.title: in-toto Attestation Framework — Statement layer, v1
sources.relevance: Layered Envelope/Statement/Predicate model; subject is a set of ResourceDescriptors matched purely by digest regardless of content type and assumed immutable, with predicateType as a TypeURI. Grounds digest-based evidence identity, typed predicates and separation of the signed envelope from the asserted content.

sources.title: CiTO, the Citation Typing Ontology
sources.relevance: Roughly 41 sub-properties of cito:cites providing a governed vocabulary of support relations — citesAsEvidence, citesAsAuthority, citesAsDataSource, supports, confirms, agreesWith, disputes, disagreesWith, refutes, corrects, extends, qualifies, usesMethodIn — and the factual vs rhetorical (positive/neutral/negative) classification.

sources.title: GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) Working Group
sources.version_or_date: Working group established 2000; methodology series in J Clin Epidemiol from 2011, criteria update 2023
sources.relevance: Four-level certainty of evidence (high/moderate/low/very low) with explicit rating-down domains (risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias) and rating-up factors (large effect, dose-response, plausible opposing bias), and separation of certainty from strength and direction of recommendation.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
sources.organization: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.version_or_date: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024; OJ publication 12 July 2024
sources.relevance: Article 11 requires technical documentation; Article 12(1) requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over the system lifetime, with Article 12(3) prescribing minimum log content for biometric identification (use periods with timestamps, reference database, matching input data, identity of verifying persons). Grounds mandated machine-generated evidence and its documentation.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)
sources.organization: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.relevance: Article 5(1)(d) accuracy, 5(1)(e) storage limitation (identifiable form no longer than necessary), 5(2) accountability (controller must be able to demonstrate compliance), Article 30 records of processing, and Article 17 erasure with the 17(3)(e) exemption for establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims — the governing tension between immutable evidence and deletion rights.

sources.title: Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 901 — Authenticating or Identifying Evidence
sources.organization: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (publishing the U.S. Federal Rules of Evidence)
sources.version_or_date: Restyled rules effective 1 December 2011, as amended
sources.relevance: Requires the proponent to produce evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it is, and enumerates authentication methods including distinctive characteristics, public records, ancient documents/data, and evidence describing a process or system and showing it produces an accurate result. Grounds authentication, originality and sufficiency-of-foundation questions.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.relevance: Control catalogue including the Audit and Accountability (AU) family, which establishes organisational requirements for event logging, audit record content, protection of audit information, non-repudiation, time stamps and audit record retention; grounds the governance controls around evidence records treated as accountability artefacts.

sources.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act — Article 19: Automatically generated logs
sources.organization: Future of Life Institute (AI Act Explorer)
sources.version_or_date: Article text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as published; accessed 2026
sources.relevance: Used only to obtain the Article 19 retention floor: providers must keep automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, unless otherwise provided by Union or national law, in particular data-protection law. Retention floor must be re-verified against the OJ text before operational use.

sources.title: FHIR Resource Evidence
sources.relevance: Machine-interpretable evidence record with identifiers, status lifecycle, authors, reviewers, endorsers, description, assertion, notes, related artifacts, statistics, study and synthesis types, and a certainty element for overall and subcomponent quality.

sources.title: Federal Rules of Evidence Rule 401. Test for Relevant Evidence
sources.organization: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.relevance: Defines relevance as a relation: evidence is relevant only if it tends to make a fact of consequence more or less probable. Relevancy is not an inherent property of an item.

sources.title: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification
sources.organization: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
sources.relevance: Tamper-evident manifests binding hashed assertions, claims, signatures and timestamps to assets, with validation states, redaction, unique identifiers and an explicit refusal to judge provenance as good or bad.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.relevance: Forensic process guidance for collecting, examining and analyzing digital sources while preserving integrity for later reliance, from an IT and incident-response view rather than a law-enforcement view.

bundles.name: Claim–Support Structure
bundles.description: The argument skeleton: how a support record binds to exactly one supported claim or decision, what kind of support relation is asserted, what reasoning licenses the conclusion, and how contrary evidence is registered and resolved.
bundles.rationale: An assurance case is a top-level claim plus systematic argumentation plus the evidence and explicit assumptions underlying it, so support cannot be modelled as a bare list of attachments; the inference step and its justification are separately addressable and separately confidence-bearing.

layers.name: Support Binding and Relation Typing
layers.description: How the mixin attaches to its host assertion and what typed relation each evidence item bears to it.

findings.name: Host binding and scope of support
findings.description: Identifies the single claim, decision or assertion the record supports, the part of it in scope, and the effect of host revision. Evidence attaches to a specific claim, not to a document.

questions.text: Which single claim, decision or assertion does this record support, and by which stable identifier in which master system?
Does the support apply to the whole host assertion or only to a named component, qualifier or numeric bound within it?
Can one evidence item support several claims by reference without being copied, and how is that many-to-many reuse represented?
When the host assertion is revised or superseded, does the support record carry over, lapse, or require re-affirmation?

data_elements.name: Support record identifier
data_elements.description: Stable identifier of this evidence/rationale record, distinct from the identifier of the host assertion and from any evidence item.

data_elements.name: Supported subject reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the host claim, decision, classification or measurement whose support is being recorded.

data_elements.name: Supported aspect path
data_elements.description: Pointer to the part of the host assertion actually supported when support is partial.

data_elements.name: Reuse mode
data_elements.description: Whether the evidence item is referenced in place or embedded as a copy in this support record.

data_elements.name: Host-revision carryover policy
data_elements.description: Declared behaviour of the support record when the host assertion changes version.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Binding is pure referential structure held on the host record; it produces no separable document, and materialising it as a file would create a second identity for a relationship that must remain single-valued.

findings.name: Typed support relation
findings.description: The declared relation each evidence item bears to the supported subject — supports, corroborates, is authority for, qualifies, disputes, refutes — drawn from a named vocabulary rather than free text.

questions.text: Which governed vocabulary and version supplies the relation term, and what is its IRI?
Is the relation supportive, neutral/informative or contrary, and is that polarity asserted or derived from the vocabulary?
Who asserted that this item stands in this relation to the claim, as distinct from who created the item?
Does the relation carry a weight or contribution, and on what scale is that weight expressed?

data_elements.name: Relation type code
data_elements.description: Term identifying the support relation, e.g. an equivalent of citesAsEvidence, citesAsAuthority, supports, qualifies, disputes or refutes.

data_elements.name: Relation vocabulary IRI
data_elements.description: IRI and version of the vocabulary from which the relation term is drawn.

data_elements.name: Relation polarity
data_elements.description: Supportive, informative/neutral or contrary classification of the relation.

data_elements.name: Relation asserter
data_elements.description: Agent responsible for asserting the support relation itself.

data_elements.name: Relation weight
data_elements.description: Optional contribution weight of this item to the overall support, meaningless without its declared scale.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The typed relation is an edge attribute in a graph; it has no independent media form. Its vocabulary is an external artefact owned by the vocabulary publisher, referenced by IRI rather than reproduced.

findings.name: Relevance to a fact of consequence
findings.description: Records the relevancy analysis without treating relevance as an inherent property of the item and without confusing it with sufficiency of the whole body of evidence.

questions.text: Does this item have any tendency to make the stated fact more or less probable than it would be without the item?
Is the fact to which the item is directed of consequence in determining the host action or decision?
Does probative value depend on a missing condition of fact, such as whether a statement was heard, that must be recorded as conditional relevance?

data_elements.name: Has probative tendency
data_elements.description: Whether the item tends to change the probability of the fact.

data_elements.name: Probability direction
data_elements.description: More probable or less probable.

data_elements.name: Is of consequence
data_elements.description: Whether the fact is of consequence in determining the action.

data_elements.name: Conditional relevance
data_elements.description: Optional condition of fact on which relevancy depends.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Relevance is a recorded relation and legal-reasoning analysis, not an exhibit.

layers.name: Reasoning, Assumptions and Challenge
layers.description: The inference that licenses moving from evidence to claim, the assumptions and context conditions it depends on, the alternatives rejected, and the counter-evidence and defeaters raised against it.

findings.name: Inference, warrant and argumentation scheme
findings.description: The reasoning step deriving the claim from its premises under a specified context, expressed as a justification, together with the scheme or rule applied and its defeasibility.

questions.text: What warrant licenses the step from these premises to this claim, stated so a reviewer can attack the step rather than the premises?
Which argumentation scheme or inference rule is applied, and from which catalogue and version is it drawn?
Is the inference deductive, inductive, abductive or statistical, and what conditions would defeat it without any premise being false?
Is the reasoning machine-checkable, reviewer-checkable, or asserted only, and what evidence supports that classification?
If no evidence item is attached, on what basis other than evidence does the conclusion rest, and is that flagged to consumers?

data_elements.name: Rationale statement
data_elements.description: Human-readable justification of the inference step in the declared context.

data_elements.name: Inference mode
data_elements.description: Deductive, inductive, abductive, statistical, analogical or authority-based character of the step.

data_elements.name: Argumentation scheme reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the scheme or inference rule instantiated, with catalogue and version.

data_elements.name: Defeat condition
data_elements.description: Stated condition under which the inference would no longer license the claim.

data_elements.name: Assumption-only support flag
data_elements.description: True when the claim rests on assumptions and reasoning with no attached evidence item.

artifacts.name: Argument structure record
artifacts.description: Serialised graph of claims, inference steps, justifications and evidence references expressing the structured argumentation for one supported claim, independent of any particular graphical notation.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by the support-record identifier plus an argument-version label; where an external assurance-case tool is the master system, its identifier takes precedence, otherwise a Dimension-assigned ULID.

findings.name: Assumptions, context conditions and rejected alternatives
findings.description: The explicit assumptions the argument depends on, the scope conditions bounding its validity, and the options considered and rejected with reasons — the part of rationale that explains why not something else.

questions.text: Which assumptions must hold for this support to stand, and is each validated, accepted-without-validation or known-unverifiable?
Under what context, population, environment or time window does the support hold, and where does it explicitly not apply?
Which alternative claims, options or interpretations were considered and rejected, and on what stated ground was each rejected?
What observable change would invalidate an assumption, and who is accountable for monitoring it?

data_elements.name: Explicit assumption
data_elements.description: A stated assumption underlying the argumentation, recorded explicitly rather than left implicit.

data_elements.name: Assumption status
data_elements.description: Validated, accepted, contested or unverifiable status of an assumption.

data_elements.name: Context condition
data_elements.description: Specified context within which the inference is claimed to hold.

data_elements.name: Alternative considered
data_elements.description: An option or interpretation that was evaluated and not adopted.

data_elements.name: Rejection reason
data_elements.description: Stated reason an alternative was not adopted, paired with the alternative.

data_elements.name: Assumption review due
data_elements.description: Date by which an assumption must be re-examined.

artifacts.name: Decision rationale record
artifacts.description: Durable record attached to a decision capturing context, options considered, the option chosen, rejection reasons and the assumptions the decision depends on.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential rationale record number within the owning decision register, qualified by the register identifier; the decision model's identifier is authoritative where one exists.

findings.name: Counter-evidence, defeaters and their resolution
findings.description: Registration of evidence and arguments that rebut the claim, undercut the inference or undermine a premise, and the record of how each was adjudicated or left open.

questions.text: What contrary or non-confirming evidence is known to exist, including evidence sought but not found?
Does each challenge rebut the claim, undercut the inference, or undermine a premise?
Who adjudicated the conflict, under what authority and by what stated rule of preference?
What conflict remains unresolved, and is that residual disclosed to consumers of the claim?
How is selective inclusion of only confirming evidence detected and prevented for this record?

data_elements.name: Counter-evidence reference
data_elements.description: Reference to an evidence item bearing a contrary relation to the supported subject.

data_elements.name: Defeater type
data_elements.description: Rebutting, undercutting or undermining character of the challenge.

data_elements.name: Resolution decision
data_elements.description: Outcome of adjudicating the conflict, including 'unresolved'.

data_elements.name: Resolving authority
data_elements.description: Agent or body that adjudicated the conflict.

data_elements.name: Residual conflict flag
data_elements.description: True when a material conflict remains open after adjudication.

data_elements.name: Selective-reporting judgement
data_elements.description: Assessment of whether contrary evidence is likely to be missing from the record.

artifacts.name: Conflict adjudication record
artifacts.description: Record of a challenge to the claim or its inference, the arguments on each side, the deciding authority and the outcome, retained whether or not the challenge succeeded.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential challenge number within the support record, prefixed by the support-record identifier; adjudicating-body case number takes precedence when one exists.

bundles.name: Evidence Item, Anchoring and Custody
bundles.description: The evidence item as an addressable thing: its identity and form, where in a source it is anchored and how faithfully it was excerpted, how it was acquired, and the custody record that makes it auditable.
bundles.rationale: Digest-based subject matching treats artefacts as immutable and identifies them by content, while annotation selectors address parts of mutable resources; evidence handling separately requires an unbroken chain of custody with auditability, repeatability and reproducibility. All three are needed and none subsumes the others.

layers.name: Evidence Identity and Form
layers.description: How an evidence item is identified and classified independently of where it is stored.

findings.name: Evidence item identity
findings.description: Assignment and precedence of identifiers for an evidence item, separation of the item from the record describing it, and content-digest identity for immutable items.

questions.text: Which identifier is authoritative for this item: a master-system identifier, a governed global identifier or IRI, or a Dimension-assigned UUID/ULID?
Which identifier denotes the physical or digital item, and which denotes the record describing it?
Is the item immutable and therefore identifiable by content digest, or mutable and identifiable only by reference plus captured state?
When the item is revised, is a new identity minted or a version label appended, and how is the prior version reachable?
How are duplicate submissions of the same underlying item detected and merged without losing distinct custody histories?

data_elements.name: Evidence item identifier
data_elements.description: Authoritative identifier of the item, assigned by precedence: master-system identifier, then governed global identifier/IRI, then Dimension-assigned UUID or ULID.

data_elements.name: Identifier scheme
data_elements.description: Scheme and issuing authority of the identifier, required to interpret it.

data_elements.name: Evidence record identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the descriptive record, always distinct from the item identifier.

data_elements.name: Immutability flag
data_elements.description: Whether the item is treated as immutable, licensing digest-based identity.

data_elements.name: Version label
data_elements.description: Version designation where the item is versioned rather than re-identified.

data_elements.name: Duplicate-of reference
data_elements.description: Link to a previously registered item found to be the same underlying thing.

artifacts.name: Evidence item
artifacts.description: The addressable thing offered in support: a file, message, image, dataset extract, signed attestation, physical exhibit or recorded testimony, held or referenced under a stable identifier.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Master-system identifier where the item originates in a system of record; otherwise governed IRI; otherwise Dimension-assigned ULID, always paired with a content digest for immutable digital items.

findings.name: Evidence form and modality
findings.description: Classification of the item by evidentiary form (documentary, testimonial, observational, computational, attestation, physical) and by medium and encoding, and whether it is an original or a copy.

questions.text: Which evidentiary form does the item take, and from which governed taxonomy is that class drawn?
What media type, encoding and structural profile does the item use, and is it self-describing?
Is this the original, a forensic image, a derived rendering or a summary, and where is the original if not held?
Does the form change the handling, integrity or admissibility obligations that apply to the item?
Is the item a composite of separately addressable parts, and is each part independently identified and hashed?

data_elements.name: Evidence class
data_elements.description: Documentary, testimonial, observational/measured, computational/derived, attestation or physical classification.

data_elements.name: Media type
data_elements.description: Registered media type and, where relevant, format profile of a digital item.

data_elements.name: Original or copy
data_elements.description: Whether the held artefact is the original, an acquired image, a derived rendering or a summary.

data_elements.name: Component part reference
data_elements.description: Reference to an independently addressable part of a composite item.

data_elements.name: Handling regime
data_elements.description: Handling and preservation regime triggered by the item's form.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Form and modality are classifying attributes of the evidence item artefact already declared in this bundle; minting a second artefact for the classification would duplicate identity for the same physical or digital thing.

layers.name: Source Anchoring and Excerpt Fidelity
layers.description: Precise addressing of the part of a source relied on, capture of the source state, and the transformation chain from source to the excerpt actually used.

findings.name: Source anchor and locator
findings.description: Identification of the source resource, the selector addressing the relevant part, and the state of the source at the time of reliance so the anchor survives later change.

questions.text: Exactly which part of the source is relied on, expressed by which selector type and value?
What was the state of the source when it was relied on, and how is that state re-obtainable?
How is it detected that the source changed after anchoring, and what happens to the support when it has?
What is recorded when the item has no source anchor at all, such as a direct sensor reading or live testimony?
If the source becomes unavailable or paywalled, what preserved surrogate stands in and with what authority?

data_elements.name: Source reference
data_elements.description: Identifier of the source resource, resolved in a sibling source model rather than described here.

data_elements.name: Selector type
data_elements.description: Kind of selector used, such as fragment, text-quote, text-position, range, CSS, XPath or data-position.

data_elements.name: Selector value
data_elements.description: Structured selector payload, including prefix and suffix context for quote selectors.

data_elements.name: Source state timestamp
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time of the source representation relied on, with explicit offset or Z.

data_elements.name: Anchor drift status
data_elements.description: Whether the anchor still resolves to the content originally selected.

data_elements.name: Anchor-absent reason
data_elements.description: Stated reason the item carries no source anchor.

artifacts.name: Source snapshot
artifacts.description: Captured representation of the source as it stood at the time of reliance, retained so the anchor remains resolvable after the live source changes or disappears.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content digest of the capture plus the capture timestamp; where a memento or archive service is the master system, its archived-resource identifier takes precedence.

findings.name: Excerpt fidelity and transformation chain
findings.description: Whether what is relied on is a verbatim quotation or a transformed derivative, which transformations were applied by which agent, and how the excerpt can be checked back against the source.

questions.text: Is the relied-on text or data a verbatim quotation from the source, a translation, an OCR output, a redaction or a paraphrase?
Which transformation steps were applied between the source and the excerpt, in what order, and by which agent or tool?
How can a third party verify the excerpt against the source, and what is the outcome of the last such check?
In what language and script is the excerpt, and if translated, who translated it and is the original retained?
Does the excerpt preserve the qualifications, negations and scope present in the source, and who confirmed that?

data_elements.name: Excerpt
data_elements.description: The quoted or extracted content actually relied on.

data_elements.name: Fidelity mode
data_elements.description: Verbatim, translated, machine-transcribed, redacted or paraphrased character of the excerpt.

data_elements.name: Transformation step
data_elements.description: An ordered transformation applied between source and excerpt, modelled as a derivation.

data_elements.name: Transformation agent
data_elements.description: Person, organisation or software agent that performed a transformation step.

data_elements.name: Language tag
data_elements.description: Language and script tag of the excerpt.

data_elements.name: Fidelity check result
data_elements.description: Outcome of comparing the excerpt against the anchored source.

artifacts.name: Excerpt record
artifacts.description: Retained excerpt together with its anchor, fidelity mode and transformation chain, so the quotation can be audited without re-fetching the source.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Digest of the excerpt content combined with the anchor identifier; no independent external identifier is assumed.

layers.name: Acquisition and Chain of Custody
layers.description: How the item was obtained and by what method and instrument, and the unbroken custody record from acquisition to present.

findings.name: Acquisition method and instrument
findings.description: The method, tool, settings and operator used to obtain the item, and whether the process is one shown to produce an accurate result.

questions.text: By which of identification, collection, acquisition or preservation was the item obtained, and what method was used?
Which instrument or tool, at which version and configuration, produced the item?
Who performed the acquisition, under what role and with what demonstrated competence?
Is the process one shown to produce an accurate result, and where is that showing recorded?
Where and under what conditions was the item acquired, to the precision the case requires?

data_elements.name: Acquisition method
data_elements.description: Coded method by which the item was obtained.

data_elements.name: Tool and version
data_elements.description: Instrument, software or device with version used in acquisition.

data_elements.name: Acquiring agent
data_elements.description: Agent that performed the acquisition, in a declared role.

data_elements.name: Acquisition time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time of acquisition with explicit offset or Z.

data_elements.name: Collection location
data_elements.description: Place, system or endpoint from which the item was collected.

data_elements.name: Method validation reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the record showing the process produces an accurate result.

artifacts.name: Acquisition log
artifacts.description: Contemporaneous record of the acquisition event: method, tool and version, parameters, operator, time and location, sufficient for an independent party to repeat the acquisition.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential acquisition number within the acquiring organisation's case or batch, qualified by that organisation's identifier; instrument-assigned run identifier takes precedence where the instrument is the master system.

findings.name: Chain of custody and handling
findings.description: The custody record from the moment the item was acquired: who held it, when, what integrity check accompanied each transfer, and whether any gap exists. Custody is physical, logical and documentary.

questions.text: What sequence of custody events exists from acquisition to now, and is any interval unaccounted for?
Who held or controlled the item during each interval, and under what authority did control transfer?
What integrity value or seal was recorded at each transfer, and did it verify on receipt?
Which custody modes apply — physical storage, logical seals and hashes, documentary access logs — and who maintains each?
For how long after the evidence ceases to be needed must the custody record itself be preserved?

data_elements.name: Custody event
data_elements.description: A single acquisition, transfer, access, storage or disposal event in the custody chain.

data_elements.name: Custodian
data_elements.description: Agent holding or controlling the item during an interval.

data_elements.name: Custody event time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time of a custody event with explicit offset or Z.

data_elements.name: Transfer seal or hash
data_elements.description: Integrity value, seal or qualified timestamp recorded at a custody transfer.

data_elements.name: Custody gap flag
data_elements.description: True when an interval in the chain is unaccounted for.

data_elements.name: Custody record retention
data_elements.description: Time until which the custody record itself must be preserved, typically outlasting the evidence.

artifacts.name: Chain of custody log
artifacts.description: Append-only sequence of custody events maintained from acquisition and preserved beyond the evidence lifetime, covering physical, logical and documentary custody.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Monotonically increasing event sequence number within the evidence item identifier; each entry additionally carries the custodian identifier and an RFC 3339 timestamp.

bundles.name: Provenance, Attribution and Time
bundles.description: Where the evidence came from, who is responsible for it and for the assertion of support, and the separated time points that let a reader judge currency and ordering.
bundles.rationale: Provenance records generation, derivation and attribution, and treats a provenance bundle as itself an entity so that provenance can be attributed and its trustworthiness assessed; primary-source, quotation and revision relations are distinguished, and generation, usage, start and end times are separately expressible.

layers.name: Origin, Derivation and Attribution
layers.description: The lineage of the evidence item and the responsibility relations attached to it and to the support assertion.

findings.name: Derivation chain and primary source
findings.description: The chain from the item back to its origin, distinguishing primary source produced by an agent with direct experience from quotation, revision and downstream derivation.

questions.text: Which preceding entity, produced by an agent with direct experience of the matter, is the primary source of this item?
What derivation, quotation and revision steps connect this item to that origin, and which activity generated each step?
Is the item primary, secondary or tertiary relative to the claim, and by whose classification?
Does the lineage contain a cycle or converge on a single upstream origin shared with items counted as independent?
When the item was composed from other assets, is each ingredient's own provenance retained rather than flattened?

data_elements.name: Primary source reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the preceding entity produced by an agent with direct experience of the subject matter.

data_elements.name: Derived-from reference
data_elements.description: Reference to an entity from which this item was derived, quoted or revised.

data_elements.name: Derivation kind
data_elements.description: Whether the step is a general derivation, a quotation or a revision.

data_elements.name: Generating activity
data_elements.description: Activity whose completion produced the item.

data_elements.name: Source tier
data_elements.description: Primary, secondary or tertiary standing of the item relative to the claim.

data_elements.name: Ingredient reference
data_elements.description: Reference to a constituent asset incorporated into a composed item, whose own provenance is retained.

artifacts.name: Provenance graph
artifacts.description: Serialised graph of entities, activities and agents with derivation, generation and attribution relations for the evidence items in this support record; itself an entity that can be attributed and dated.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Named bundle identifier assigned by the Dimension, distinct from the identifiers of the entities it describes, enabling provenance-of-provenance.

findings.name: Attribution, responsibility and independence
findings.description: Which agents bear responsibility for the item and for the assertion that it supports the claim, on whose behalf they acted, and whether they are independent of the outcome.

questions.text: To which agent is the item attributed, and which agent asserted that it supports the claim?
Did the agent act on behalf of another agent who retains responsibility, and is that delegation recorded?
Is the responsible agent a person, an organisation or a software agent, and does that change the weight given?
Is the agent independent of the outcome the claim supports, and what interests are declared?
Is the item self-reported by the party whose claim it supports, and is that flagged rather than silently equated with third-party evidence?

data_elements.name: Attributed-to agent
data_elements.description: Agent to whom responsibility for the item's existence is ascribed.

data_elements.name: Acted on behalf of
data_elements.description: Agent on whose behalf the responsible agent acted, retaining some responsibility.

data_elements.name: Agent kind
data_elements.description: Person, organisation or software agent classification.

data_elements.name: Interest declaration
data_elements.description: Declared interests of the responsible or asserting agent relevant to the claim.

data_elements.name: Self-reported flag
data_elements.description: True when the item originates from the party benefiting from the claim.

data_elements.name: Competence evidence
data_elements.description: Reference to qualification, accreditation or training evidence for the responsible agent.

artifacts.name: Interest and independence declaration
artifacts.description: Signed declaration by an asserting or appraising agent of interests, affiliations and relationships bearing on independence, retained alongside the appraisal it qualifies.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Declaring agent identifier plus the identifier of the support record or appraisal it qualifies, plus an RFC 3339 declaration timestamp.

layers.name: Temporal Frame and Currency
layers.description: Separated time points, clock quality, and the window within which the support remains adequate.

findings.name: Separated time points and clock quality
findings.description: Distinct recording of when the fact occurred, when it was observed, when it was ingested and when support was asserted, each in RFC 3339 with explicit offset, plus the clock source that produced them.

questions.text: Which distinct time points are recorded — event, observation, ingestion, assertion, verification — and which are unknown?
Does every time value carry seconds and an explicit numeric offset or Z, and is -00:00 used only where the local offset is genuinely unknown?
What clock produced each timestamp, with what traceability and accuracy?
How is a partially known time expressed without inventing precision, for example a known date but unknown time?
When two records disagree on ordering because their clocks differ, which ordering rule governs?

data_elements.name: Event time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time at which the fact evidenced actually occurred.

data_elements.name: Observation time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time at which the fact was observed or measured.

data_elements.name: Record/ingestion time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time at which the item entered the holding system.

data_elements.name: Assertion time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time at which the support relation was asserted.

data_elements.name: Clock source
data_elements.description: Identification of the clock or time service that produced a timestamp.

data_elements.name: Time precision
data_elements.description: Declared precision of a time value so that unknown components are not read as zero.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Time points are scalar attributes of other artefacts (evidence item, custody event, verification event) and are meaningless when detached from them; a separate time artefact would introduce a spurious identity and invite divergence from the record it stamps.

findings.name: Validity window, staleness and supersession
findings.description: The period over which the support is asserted to hold, the re-verification cadence, and how superseding evidence replaces it without erasing the prior state.

questions.text: From when until when is this support asserted to hold, and is the end open or fixed?
How often must the support be re-verified for its purpose, and when is the next re-verification due?
At what point does the support count as stale, and what does a consumer see when it is?
Which later support record supersedes this one, and is the superseded record retained and still resolvable?
What invalidates the evidence item itself, as distinct from the support lapsing, and how is that recorded?

data_elements.name: Valid from
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 start of the period over which the support is asserted to hold.

data_elements.name: Valid until
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 end of the asserted validity period, absent when open-ended.

data_elements.name: Revalidation due
data_elements.description: Date by which re-verification must occur for the support to remain current.

data_elements.name: Staleness status
data_elements.description: Current, due-for-review or stale standing of the support record.

data_elements.name: Superseded by
data_elements.description: Reference to the support record that replaces this one.

data_elements.name: Invalidation time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time marking the start of destruction, cessation or expiry of the evidence entity.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Validity and supersession are state attributes carried on the support record and expressed through references to successor records; materialising a separate 'validity artefact' would split a single record's state across two identities.

bundles.name: Integrity, Attestation and Verification
bundles.description: Whether the evidence is what it purports to be and has not changed: content binding by digest, signatures and attestations, trusted timestamps, verification events, and reproducibility of derived evidence.
bundles.rationale: A hard binding lets a validator confirm both that the manifest belongs with the asset and that the asset has not been modified; attestation subjects are matched purely by digest; a time-stamp authority establishes that a datum existed before a particular time. Verification of integrity is explicitly not evaluation of the truth of the claims carried.

layers.name: Cryptographic Binding and Attestation
layers.description: Digests, signatures and timestamps that make an evidence record tamper-evident and its time of existence provable.

findings.name: Content digest and hard binding
findings.description: What is hashed, under which algorithm and canonical form, and how the binding survives storage-format change. Digest identity applies only to items treated as immutable.

questions.text: Which digest algorithms are recorded, and does the record permit more than one to support algorithm agility?
Exactly what bytes or structure does the digest cover, and under what canonicalisation?
Does a hard binding exist that ties the support record to this specific item rather than merely naming it?
What happens to the binding when the item is transcoded, re-encoded or migrated between stores?
For items that cannot be hashed, such as physical exhibits or live testimony, what stands in for content binding?

data_elements.name: Digest algorithm
data_elements.description: Named hash algorithm used, recorded alongside each digest value.

data_elements.name: Digest value
data_elements.description: Computed hash of the covered content.

data_elements.name: Canonicalisation method
data_elements.description: Method fixing the byte form hashed, without which digests are not comparable.

data_elements.name: Covered range
data_elements.description: Byte ranges, boxes or structural extent covered by the digest.

data_elements.name: Hard binding present
data_elements.description: True when at least one binding lets a validator confirm the record belongs with this item and the item is unmodified.

data_elements.name: Binding substitute
data_elements.description: Non-cryptographic substitute used where hashing is impossible, such as a tamper-evident seal and custody record.

artifacts.name: Integrity manifest
artifacts.description: Set of digests and covered ranges for the evidence items and excerpts in a support record, referenced by hashed URIs so that a reference cannot silently point at changed content.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Digest of the manifest itself, referenced by a hashed URI combining location and hash; no external identifier assumed.

findings.name: Signature and attestation
findings.description: Who cryptographically asserted the record, under which securing mechanism, what the signature covers, and how signer trust and revocation are established.

questions.text: Which agent signed, with which key or certificate, and how is that signer identity resolved to a known party?
Which securing mechanism is used, embedded or enveloping, and is more than one required?
What exactly does the signature cover — the claim, the assertion set, the payload — and what is deliberately outside it?
Against which trust list or policy is the signer accepted, and who curates that list?
How is revocation or expiry of the signing credential detected, and does it retroactively invalidate the record?

data_elements.name: Signature value
data_elements.description: Cryptographic signature securing the record or attestation envelope.

data_elements.name: Signing agent
data_elements.description: Agent whose key produced the signature, distinct from the agent asserting support.

data_elements.name: Securing mechanism
data_elements.description: Embedded or enveloping securing mechanism identifier.

data_elements.name: Signature coverage
data_elements.description: Statement of what content the signature covers.

data_elements.name: Revocation status
data_elements.description: Current status of the signing credential at last check.

data_elements.name: Trust list reference
data_elements.description: Trust list or policy against which the signer is evaluated.

artifacts.name: Signed attestation envelope
artifacts.description: Envelope carrying a typed statement about identified subjects together with its signature, keeping the signed payload separable from the signature and from the predicate content.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Subject digests plus predicate type URI identify what is attested; the envelope itself is addressed by its own digest, with issuer-assigned credential identifier taking precedence where present.

findings.name: Trusted timestamp and temporal proof
findings.description: Third-party attestation that the evidence existed before a stated time, with the accuracy and policy under which it was issued, and the long-term validity strategy.

questions.text: Is there a third-party timestamp proving the item existed before a stated time, and if not, why is a self-asserted time considered sufficient?
Which authority issued the token, under which policy identifier, and what serial number does it carry?
What generation time and accuracy does the token assert, and is that precision adequate for the ordering the claim depends on?
How does the record stay verifiable after signing credentials expire or algorithms weaken?
What would distinguish a genuine token from a backdated one if the authority's key were compromised?

data_elements.name: Timestamp token
data_elements.description: Signed token binding a hash of the record to a generation time.

data_elements.name: Timestamp authority
data_elements.description: Identity of the trusted third party that issued the token.

data_elements.name: Token generation time
data_elements.description: Time asserted by the authority at which the token was created.

data_elements.name: Timestamp accuracy
data_elements.description: Declared deviation around the generation time.

data_elements.name: Timestamp policy identifier
data_elements.description: Policy under which the authority issued the token.

data_elements.name: Long-term validation strategy
data_elements.description: Declared approach to preserving verifiability past credential expiry or algorithm weakening.

artifacts.name: Timestamp token artefact
artifacts.description: Retained time-stamp token proving the bound record existed before the asserted time, stored so it remains verifiable independently of the issuing service.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Authority identifier plus the token serial number assigned by that authority; the message imprint links the token to the record it stamps.

layers.name: Verification Events and Reproducibility
layers.description: The record of checks actually performed on the evidence, and whether derived or computed evidence can be independently re-derived.

findings.name: Verification events and current status
findings.description: Each verification is an event with an actor, method, time and outcome; the current status is derived from events, not asserted independently, and integrity verification is kept separate from truth of the claim.

questions.text: When was the record last verified, by which agent, using which method and tool version?
What was the outcome of each verification step, and which specific step failed when the outcome was negative?
Does the verification status assert only integrity and signer validity, and is it clearly not a statement that the claim is true?
For how long is a verification result relied on before it must be repeated?
Can a party other than the issuer verify the record with only the exported package, and what does that require?

data_elements.name: Verification event
data_elements.description: A single verification attempt with actor, method, time and result.

data_elements.name: Verification time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time of a verification event.

data_elements.name: Verifier
data_elements.description: Agent that performed the verification.

data_elements.name: Verification method
data_elements.description: Named method and tool version used to verify.

data_elements.name: Verification outcome
data_elements.description: Result of the verification, including partial success with named failed steps.

data_elements.name: Independent verifiability
data_elements.description: True when a third party can verify using only the exported package.

artifacts.name: Verification report
artifacts.description: Report of a verification run over a support record: manifest located, signature checked, timestamp checked, assertions validated, bindings compared, with per-step outcomes.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential run number within the verifying system, qualified by that system's identifier and the digest of the record verified.

findings.name: Reproducibility and method replay
findings.description: For computed, analysed or derived evidence, whether the same result is obtainable by the same person with the same method (repeatability) and by a different person with a different setup (reproducibility).

questions.text: Can an independent party re-derive this evidence, and has anyone actually done so with what result?
Which inputs, parameters, code versions and environment are recorded, and are they sufficient to re-run?
Is the derivation deterministic, and if not, what is the expected variation and its source?
What prevents reproduction — licensed data, unavailable hardware, expired credentials, non-public source — and is that disclosed?
Is the record claiming repeatability, reproducibility, or neither, and on what basis?

data_elements.name: Method description
data_elements.description: Description of the derivation method at a level allowing re-execution.

data_elements.name: Input manifest
data_elements.description: Identified and digested inputs consumed by the derivation.

data_elements.name: Environment descriptor
data_elements.description: Execution environment, code versions and configuration used.

data_elements.name: Determinism flag
data_elements.description: Whether re-running the method on the same inputs yields identical output.

data_elements.name: Replication result
data_elements.description: Outcome of an attempted independent reproduction.

data_elements.name: Reproduction blocker
data_elements.description: Stated obstacle preventing independent reproduction.

artifacts.name: Reproduction package
artifacts.description: Self-contained bundle of inputs, method, parameters and environment description enabling an independent party to attempt re-derivation of computed evidence.
media_or_form: notebook or script set with input manifest
artifacts.identity_strategy: Digest of the package plus the identifier of the evidence item it reproduces; a build or pipeline run identifier from the master system takes precedence where one exists.

findings.name: Authentication foundation
findings.description: The proponent must produce support sufficient to find that the item is what it is claimed to be, using one or more recognized methods such as witness knowledge, distinctive characteristics, public-record custody, or process-or-system accuracy.

questions.text: What is the item claimed to be, and what would count as it being that thing?
Which authentication method or methods are offered, and are they examples under a governing rule or another statute-provided method?
Has authentication been distinguished from later bars such as hearsay, privilege or prejudice that can still exclude an authenticated item?

data_elements.name: Claimed identity of item
data_elements.description: What the proponent claims the item is.

data_elements.name: Authentication methods
data_elements.description: Non-exclusive methods used to authenticate or identify the item.

data_elements.name: Authentication status
data_elements.description: Whether a sufficient foundation has been recorded.

data_elements.name: Remaining bars
data_elements.description: Noted bars that authentication does not remove.

artifacts.name: Authentication foundation record
artifacts.description: Record of the method and supporting testimony or system description used to authenticate the item.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Item master identifier plus authentication-event serial.

bundles.name: Appraisal, Strength and Sufficiency
bundles.description: How strong the support is against a declared scheme, what limits it, whether it meets the threshold the decision requires, and whether apparent corroboration is genuine.
bundles.rationale: Certainty of evidence is rated against explicit domains and is separate from the strength of any recommendation drawn from it; legal sufficiency requires evidence sufficient to support a finding that an item is what it is claimed to be. Strength is therefore scheme-relative and threshold-relative, never a bare number.

layers.name: Certainty and Limitations
layers.description: Scheme-declared certainty grading and the explicit limitations that drive it.

findings.name: Certainty grading against a declared scheme
findings.description: The certainty or confidence level assigned, always paired with the identifier and version of the scheme that defines it, the domains that drove the rating and the grader.

questions.text: Which grading scheme and version defines the level assigned, and what are its permitted values?
What certainty level is assigned, and which domains caused it to be rated down or up?
Who performed the grading, when, and were they independent of the claim's proponent?
Is certainty in the evidence kept distinct from the strength and direction of any recommendation or decision drawn from it?
Can this level be compared with a level from a different scheme, and on what authority is any such mapping made?

data_elements.name: Grading scheme identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier and version of the scheme defining the certainty vocabulary; a level without this is uninterpretable.

data_elements.name: Certainty level
data_elements.description: Assigned level within the declared scheme, such as high, moderate, low or very low.

data_elements.name: Rating domain judgement
data_elements.description: Per-domain judgement driving the rating, for example risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or selective reporting.

data_elements.name: Grader
data_elements.description: Agent that assigned the certainty level.

data_elements.name: Grading time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time at which the grading was performed.

data_elements.name: Recommendation strength
data_elements.description: Strength of any recommendation drawn, recorded separately from evidence certainty.

artifacts.name: Evidence appraisal record
artifacts.description: Structured summary of the body of evidence for one claim: per-domain judgements, the resulting certainty level, the scheme applied and the reasons for each downgrade or upgrade.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Support-record identifier plus scheme identifier plus grading timestamp; where a guideline or review body is the master system, its appraisal identifier takes precedence.

findings.name: Bias, limitations and measurement reliability
findings.description: Known biases, coverage limits, indirectness and quantified uncertainty attaching to the evidence, recorded so consumers see them without re-deriving them.

questions.text: What biases are known or suspected in how this evidence was produced or selected?
What measurement error, interval or confidence attaches to any quantitative evidence, and in what units?
What population, period, geography or system does the evidence actually cover, and where is it being applied beyond that?
How are these limitations surfaced to a downstream consumer who reads only the claim?
Which limitations are known to exist but are not quantified, and is that stated rather than omitted?

data_elements.name: Bias domain
data_elements.description: Named domain in which bias is assessed.

data_elements.name: Bias judgement
data_elements.description: Assessment outcome for a bias domain, such as low, some concerns or high.

data_elements.name: Uncertainty
data_elements.description: Quantified uncertainty attaching to a measured value, with its unit and basis.

data_elements.name: Coverage limitation
data_elements.description: Stated boundary of what the evidence actually covers.

data_elements.name: Indirectness note
data_elements.description: Statement of the gap between the evidence obtained and the question asked.

data_elements.name: Unquantified limitation
data_elements.description: Known limitation for which no quantification is available.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Limitations are qualifying attributes of the appraisal record already declared in this layer. Separating them into their own artefact would allow a certainty level to circulate without its caveats, which is the specific failure this finding exists to prevent.

findings.name: Quantitative statistic support
findings.description: The numeric heart of scientific evidence: statistic type, quantity, unit, sample size, intervals, p values, model characteristics, and study or synthesis type.

questions.text: What statistic type, quantity, unit of measure and sample size are reported for this evidence bit?
What confidence intervals, p values, heterogeneity estimates and statistic-model characteristics qualify the quantity?
From what study type, and if synthesized from what synthesis type, was the statistic obtained?

data_elements.name: Statistic
data_elements.description: Machine-interpretable statistic backbone including quantity and type.

data_elements.name: Quantity
data_elements.description: Numeric result of the statistic.

data_elements.name: Sample size
data_elements.description: Sample size associated with the statistic.

data_elements.name: Study type
data_elements.description: Type of study from which the evidence was obtained.

data_elements.name: Synthesis type
data_elements.description: Type of synthesis if the evidence is derived from synthesis.

data_elements.name: Variable definitions
data_elements.description: Population, exposure, outcome and other variable roles the statistic is about.

artifacts.name: Statistic payload
artifacts.description: Computable statistic object matching a single combination of variable definitions.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Evidence resource identifier plus statistic index.

layers.name: Sufficiency, Burden and Corroboration
layers.description: Whether the assembled support clears the threshold the decision requires, and whether multiple items are genuinely independent.

findings.name: Sufficiency threshold and burden
findings.description: The standard the support must meet for this decision, who set it, whether it is met, and what would be needed if not. Sufficiency is a property of the assembled support, not of any single item.

questions.text: What standard must the support meet for this decision, and who set that standard?
Is the standard met on the evidence currently assembled, and who determined that?
If it is not met, precisely what additional evidence or reasoning would close the gap?
Which party bears the burden of producing support, and does that burden shift on any condition?
What happens operationally when a decision proceeds despite insufficient support, and how is that override recorded?

data_elements.name: Sufficiency standard
data_elements.description: Named standard or threshold the support must satisfy for this decision class.

data_elements.name: Threshold definition
data_elements.description: Operational statement of what satisfying the standard requires.

data_elements.name: Sufficiency met
data_elements.description: Whether the assembled support meets the declared standard.

data_elements.name: Sufficiency gap
data_elements.description: Description of what is missing when the standard is not met.

data_elements.name: Override flag
data_elements.description: True when a decision proceeded despite declared insufficiency.

data_elements.name: Override authority
data_elements.description: Agent who authorised proceeding despite insufficient support.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Sufficiency is a determination about a support record as a whole and is recorded as state on that record; the deliberation behind it, where written down, is captured by the decision-rationale-record and conflict-adjudication-record artefacts already declared, so a third artefact would fragment one determination.

findings.name: Corroboration and genuine independence
findings.description: Whether multiple supporting items are independent or trace to one origin, and detection of double counting and circular citation that inflate apparent support.

questions.text: How many distinct items support the claim, and how many remain after collapsing items that share an origin?
Are the supporting items independent in origin, method and agent, and on what basis is independence asserted?
Does any supporting item ultimately cite the claim it is offered to support, or cite a sibling item as its own source?
If support rests on a single item or agent, is that single-source dependency flagged to consumers?
Does convergence of independent items change the certainty level, and under which rule of the declared scheme?

data_elements.name: Corroborating item count
data_elements.description: Number of items asserted to support the claim.

data_elements.name: Effective independent count
data_elements.description: Count remaining after collapsing items sharing an upstream origin.

data_elements.name: Independence assessment
data_elements.description: Judgement of whether supporting items or agents are genuinely independent.

data_elements.name: Shared origin flag
data_elements.description: True when two or more nominally independent items trace to one origin.

data_elements.name: Circularity check result
data_elements.description: Outcome of testing the citation and derivation graph for cycles.

data_elements.name: Single-source flag
data_elements.description: True when all support traces to one item or one agent.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Independence is computed over the provenance graph artefact already declared in the provenance bundle; the analysis result is state on the support record, and duplicating it as a standalone artefact would let a stale independence count outlive the graph it was derived from.

bundles.name: Governance, Access, Retention and Interoperability
bundles.description: Who owns and approves the support record, what rights govern its reuse, who may see it and in what form, how long it is kept and how it is disposed of, how it moves through lifecycle states, and how it maps to and exchanges with external models.
bundles.rationale: Accountability requires a controller able to demonstrate compliance, storage limitation caps identifiable retention, erasure rights are qualified by a legal-claims exemption, and sectoral rules impose explicit retention floors on machine-generated logs. Evidence records therefore need an explicit governance surface rather than inheriting one.

layers.name: Ownership, Authority and Rights
layers.description: Accountable parties for the record and the rights that constrain reuse of what it contains.

findings.name: Ownership, stewardship and approving authority
findings.description: The accountable owner, the day-to-day steward, and the authority that approved the support as adequate, together with the mandate under which that approval was given.

questions.text: Which party is accountable for this support record and able to demonstrate its compliance on demand?
Who maintains the record day to day, and how does stewardship differ from ownership here?
Which authority approved the support as adequate, under what mandate, and when?
May approval authority be delegated, to whom, and does the delegating party retain responsibility?
What happens to ownership when the owning party is dissolved, reorganised or leaves, and who is the fallback?

data_elements.name: Accountable owner
data_elements.description: Party accountable for the support record and able to demonstrate its compliance.

data_elements.name: Steward
data_elements.description: Party responsible for day-to-day maintenance of the record.

data_elements.name: Approving authority
data_elements.description: Agent or body that approved the support as adequate for its purpose.

data_elements.name: Mandate reference
data_elements.description: Policy, delegation or terms of reference under which approval was given.

data_elements.name: Approval time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 time of approval with explicit offset or Z.

data_elements.name: Succession rule
data_elements.description: Declared rule for reassigning ownership when the owner ceases to exist.

artifacts.name: Approval record
artifacts.description: Record of the authority's sign-off that the assembled support is adequate for the stated purpose, including mandate, scope of approval and any conditions attached.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Sequential approval number within the approving body's register plus the support-record identifier; the approving body's own case reference takes precedence where it exists.

findings.name: Rights, licence and permitted use
findings.description: The rights attaching to source material quoted or held as evidence, what reuse and redistribution are permitted, and the attribution obligations that travel with the excerpt.

questions.text: Under what licence or legal basis is the source material held, quoted and stored?
May the evidence item or excerpt be redistributed outside the holding organisation, and to whom?
What attribution must accompany the excerpt wherever it is displayed or exported?
Does the material contain third-party rights or personal data that constrain use beyond the licence?
Do any territorial, export-control or contractual restrictions limit where the evidence may be transferred?

data_elements.name: Licence identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the licence governing the source material.

data_elements.name: Rights holder
data_elements.description: Party holding rights in the source material.

data_elements.name: Permitted use
data_elements.description: Coded scope of permitted use, quotation and redistribution.

data_elements.name: Attribution statement
data_elements.description: Attribution text that must accompany the excerpt on display or export.

data_elements.name: Contains personal data
data_elements.description: True when the evidence contains data relating to identifiable persons, triggering additional obligations.

data_elements.name: Territorial restriction
data_elements.description: Restriction on where the evidence may be stored or transferred.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Licence terms are published artefacts owned by the rights holder and are referenced by identifier rather than reproduced; copying them into this model would create an unmaintained fork of a text the Dimension has no authority to amend.

layers.name: Access, Confidentiality, Retention and Disposition
layers.description: Who may see the evidence and in what form, and how long it is kept before disposal.

findings.name: Access classification and redaction
findings.description: Classification of the support record and its items, the distinction between disclosing existence and disclosing content, and the relationship between a redacted disclosure copy and the unredacted original.

questions.text: What classification applies to the support record, and does it differ from that of individual evidence items?
May the existence of the evidence be disclosed to a party who may not see its content, and to whom?
Is legal privilege, commercial confidence or a statutory restriction claimed, by whom and on what basis?
How does a redacted disclosure copy relate to the original, and is the redaction itself recorded and reversible by authorised parties?
Is personal data in the evidence limited to what is necessary for the evidential purpose, and who reviews that?

data_elements.name: Classification
data_elements.description: Access classification applied to the support record.

data_elements.name: Access condition
data_elements.description: Condition under which a party may read the record or an item.

data_elements.name: Privilege or confidentiality claim
data_elements.description: Claimed privilege, confidentiality or statutory restriction over the material.

data_elements.name: Redaction map
data_elements.description: Record of what was removed or masked in a disclosure copy and under what authority.

data_elements.name: Disclosure copy reference
data_elements.description: Reference from the original to a derived redacted copy released to a specific audience.

data_elements.name: Redaction authority
data_elements.description: Agent who authorised the redaction.

artifacts.name: Redacted disclosure copy
artifacts.description: Derived copy of an evidence item or support record with restricted content removed or masked, linked to the unredacted original by a recorded derivation so the two are never confused.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Own identifier distinct from the original, carrying an explicit derivation link to the original identifier plus its own digest and a sequential disclosure number per recipient.

findings.name: Retention, legal hold and disposition
findings.description: How long the support record and its items are kept, the floors and caps that apply, the effect of a legal hold, how erasure requests interact with evidential need, and what remains after disposal.
